This article requires a bit of time to read, at 19 pages and moderate to hard difficulty, and a previous study context is included.

Title: Protest Song, Tradition, and the Performativity of Resistance in the Palestinian National Movement.
Object_Description (Abstract): In this chapter, David A. McDonald, in Bloomington, Indiana, writes about music as resistance, the Palestinian crisis, and the prosocial aspects of Palestinian protest song. Using ethnographic analysis of first-hand accounts, he argues that music performance and political protest are prosocial behaviors that provide a medium for social action and political solidarity. At 16 pages long, this is an easier read with little background knowledge needed, only some basics about key time periods or resistance movements.

Title: Modernity, Tradition, and Identity: The Transformation of Music-Making in Palestine, 1936 to 1948.
Object_Description (Abstract): In this paper, Issa Boulos discusses music-making in Palestine from 1936 to 1948, specifically investigating radio stations and their influence on the spread of new music genres. Utilizing historiological review of archival records, he argues that music was a vital tool for Palestinians to consolidate their identity and to connect with regional trends. This is a longer and more complex paper at 30 pages in length and moderate difficulty, mostly regarding the musicological terminology.

Title: Death-Defying Indigenous Dance:" Palest-Indian" Solidary Love.
Journal Title: The Journal of Comparative Literature and Aesthetics
Object_Description (Abstract): In Joshua M. Hall’s forthcoming article, he investigates the relationality between the North American Indigenous Peoples’ struggle and the Palestinian struggle through the lens of dance and how dance can act as a bridge between cultures. Using comparative analysis of digital ethnography, he argues that dance in indigenous cultures can be used as an act of resistance and as a sign of solidarity between indigenous groups. Some background about the American Indigenous struggle and the Palestinian struggle is required for this article. At 15 pages in length, it is a medium-length reading at medium difficulty.

Title: Ramallah ravers and Haifa hipsters: gender, class, and nation in Palestinian popular culture.
Journal Title: British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies
Object_Description (Abstract): In London scholar, Polly Wither’s article, she investigates how music and rave culture in Palestine act to subvert the dominant frameworks and structures. Using qualitative analysis between first-hand accounts, she argues that raves are only partially understood through Palestinian resistance to domination. Moderate background knowledge about rave culture is helpful. And at 21 pages, this is a longer read with moderate difficulty.

Title: Rerooted and Reimagined: Dance, Palestinian Women, and the Reclaimation of Urban Spaces
Journal Title: The Jerusalem Academy of Music and Dance
Object_Description (Abstract): In this article, Jerusalem scholar Hodel Ophir investigates Palestinian choreographer Shaden Abu Elasal and the urban settings she uses for her performances. This highlights how urban choreography serves as a mode of deepening connection to cultural land and reimagining oppressive structures. Through first-hand accounts, interviews, and choreography investigations, Ophir argues that staging dances in locations that hold significant historical meaning deepens roots to the land and brings together an identity of space. While this paper is lengthy at 18 pages, little background knowledge is needed to understand, as most topics are explained in the paper at an intermediate level of difficulty.

Title: The Three Enigmas of Palestinian Literature.
Object_Description (Abstract): In the article “The Three Enigmas of Palestinian Literature” published by the Journal of Palestinian Studies, authored by Refqa Abu-Remaileh, who is based in Ar-Rayyan, Qatar, she discusses the three enigmas in Palestinian literature utilizing an analysis of Palestinian literature. She argues that the barriers for literary scholarship revolve around rethinking conventional categorizations, canonizations, and periodizations to better understand how a national literature came from a context of exile, fragmentation, and statelessness, and how processes of cultural production operate in extranational conditions. A moderate level of background is needed on the history of Palestine in this 5-page article. Although short, it is an intermediate-level article, and most concepts are explained in the article.

Title: Country of Words: Palestinian Literature in the Digital Age of the Refugee
Object_Description (Abstract): In the article “Country of Words: Palestinian Literature in the Digital Age of Refugee” by Refqa Abu-Remaileh, published by the Journal of Arabic Literature, she explores how to welcome the scattered and unconventional elements and nature of Palestinian literature within digital humanities. Using qualitative analysis and data analysis to investigate primary and secondary sources, she argues that opening a new scope and methodology of how we engage with Palestinian literature impacts how we understand Palestinian literature and its multifaceted and fragmented nature. Using digital humanistic analysis, we can piece together a map of Palestinian literature and similar projects. Some background knowledge is needed in regard to the Palestinian diaspora and digital humanistic work; most of the material is either explained or does not go super in-depth. The article is longer at 30 pages and is of intermediate difficulty.
Keywords/Subjects/Tags: digital humanities; literature; identity; belonging; literary history

Title: "What Is This Palestine, Anyway?": Two Second-Generation Palestinian American Women Negotiate Roots and Routes.
Object_Description (Abstract): In the article ““What is This Palestine, Anyway?”: Two Second Generation Palestinian American Women Negotiate Roots and Routes” by Mai Serhan, published by the Journal of Palestinian Studies, she argues for the necessity to narrate such experiences or risk being outwritten by various Others. To achieve this, Serhan uses comparative analysis of primary sources in literature. The article is medium length at 12 pages and is beginner-friendly, with excerpts from the memoirs and the context broken down.
Keywords/Subjects/Tags: literature; narrative; identity; diaspora; belonging; memoir
